clusters.name: Why I Procrastinate
clusters.rationale: Diagnosis before tactics. Skipping this is why discipline advice has never stuck.

books.title: The Now Habit
books.author: Neil Fiore
books.why: Procrastination as an anxiety response to perfectionist pressure, not a character flaw. My book.

books.title: Solving the Procrastination Puzzle
books.author: Timothy Pychyl
books.why: Short, research-based, zero fluff. Pychyl is the academic who established procrastination as an emotion-regulation problem.

books.title: The War of Art
books.author: Steven Pressfield
books.why: Names the enemy "Resistance." One hour, quotable, useful on a bad morning.

books.title: Do Hard Things
books.author: Steve Magness
books.why: Real toughness vs. self-punishment. The antidote if discipline starts feeling like penance.

books.title: Atomic Habits
books.author: James Clear
books.why: "Identity-based habits" is already in my hierarchy. This is the source. Use it to build the reading habit itself.

books.title: Tiny Habits
books.author: BJ Fogg
books.why: Behaviour design for when motivation is simply unavailable — which is most days.

books.title: The Power of Habit
books.author: Charles Duhigg
books.why: More journalism than method. Skip unless I want the stories.

clusters.name: Attention, Dopamine & Digital Discipline
clusters.rationale: My named momentum-killer — it appears three separate times in my own dataset. This cluster also covers compulsive use of any high-dopamine input, which is the honest home for the "sexual energy" question my hierarchy raises.

books.title: Dopamine Nation
books.author: Anna Lembke
books.why: A Stanford addiction psychiatrist on the pleasure-pain balance. Covers compulsion across every input — phone, porn, food, work — with one mechanism.

books.title: Deep Work
books.author: Cal Newport
books.why: How to actually get and protect the 2–4 hour blocks I say I want.

books.title: Digital Minimalism
books.author: Cal Newport
books.why: The 30-day declutter protocol. Do it, don't just read it.

books.title: Indistractable
books.author: Nir Eyal
books.why: Internal triggers + timeboxing. A practical counterweight to Newport's absolutism.

books.title: Stolen Focus
books.author: Johann Hari
books.why: Systemic argument — attention as something taken, not lost. Good context, thin on action.

books.title: Peak Performance
books.author: Stulberg & Magness
books.why: Stress + rest = growth. Reframes discipline as energy management, which is closer to how I actually work.

books.title: Rest
books.author: Alex Soojung-Kim Pang
books.why: Rest as a deliberate skill, not a reward to be earned. Aimed at people who feel guilty stopping.

books.title: The Willpower Instinct
books.author: Kelly McGonigal
books.why: Built substantially on ego-depletion research that has failed replication. The exercises are still useful; the underlying theory should be held loosely.

books.title: Four Thousand Weeks
books.author: Oliver Burkeman
books.why: The direct, serious answer to my own sentence: "life would feel wasted if I don't achieve everything I want." Read it before I build another decade on that belief.

books.title: Essentialism
books.author: Greg McKeown
books.why: "Less but better." Repetitive, but the message lands.

books.title: Getting Things Done
books.author: David Allen
books.why: A capture system, not a philosophy. Open it when inputs overflow.

books.title: Make Time
books.author: Knapp & Zeratsky
books.why: Light and tactical. Good for a low-energy week.

clusters.name: Designing Life as a System
clusters.rationale: My Level 11 meta-layer, made readable.

books.title: The 12 Week Year
books.author: Brian Moran
books.why: Annual goals fail because twelve months is too long to feel urgency. Twelve-week cycles fix my planning horizon.

domains.name: MIND & EMOTIONAL ARCHITECTURE
domains.question: Can I live inside my own head?

books.title: Mindset
books.author: Carol Dweck
books.why: I use the phrase "growth mindset" seven times across my documents. Read the source — especially the material on **false growth mindset**, which is adopting the vocabulary without the practice. Worth checking myself against honestly.

books.title: Self-Compassion
books.author: Kristin Neff
books.why: Research-based, not soft. Neff's central finding is that self-compassion outperforms self-criticism on actual achievement — which contradicts how I currently motivate myself.

books.title: How to Be an Imperfectionist
books.author: Stephen Guise
books.why: Small, concrete exposure exercises. Cheap to read, easy to start.

books.title: The Gifts of Imperfection
books.author: Brené Brown
books.why: Letting go of who I think I'm supposed to be.

books.title: Chatter
books.author: Ethan Kross
books.why: The science of the inner voice and how to quiet it. Written for analytical internal processors — which is precisely how I described myself.

books.title: The Happiness Trap
books.author: Russ Harris
books.why: ACT in plain language. The origin of "psychological flexibility," a term already sitting in my hierarchy.

books.title: Rewire Your Anxious Brain
books.author: Pittman & Karle
books.why: Amygdala vs. cortex pathways. Mechanism-level, which an engineer's mind finds satisfying rather than patronising.

books.title: Feeling Good
books.author: David Burns
books.why: The CBT workbook. Use it on one stuck thought pattern, not as a read-through.

clusters.name: Emotional Literacy
clusters.rationale: I left "what emotion do you suppress most?" blank in my own dataset. That blank is the finding, not an oversight.

books.title: Atlas of the Heart
books.author: Brené Brown
books.why: 87 emotions, precisely distinguished. A reference for the vocabulary my hierarchy says I want ("naming emotions").

books.title: Permission to Feel
books.author: Marc Brackett
books.why: The RULER method. Systematic and staged, which suits how I learn.

books.title: Emotional Intelligence
books.author: Daniel Goleman
books.why: Foundational and worth knowing, but the popular claim that EQ predicts success far more than IQ is not well supported by the evidence. Take the framework, not the statistics.

clusters.name: Shadow, Origins & Self-Knowledge
clusters.rationale: Optional. Open only if something in 2.3 hits a nerve. Do not manufacture a wound in order to be thorough — that would be perfectionism wearing a therapy costume.

books.title: Owning Your Own Shadow
books.author: Robert A. Johnson
books.why: 90 pages. The clearest short entry to "shadow integration," which my hierarchy names without defining.

books.title: Maybe You Should Talk to Someone
books.author: Lori Gottlieb
books.why: A therapist in therapy. The gentlest possible introduction to the idea, for someone who processes everything alone.

books.title: No Bad Parts
books.author: Richard Schwartz
books.why: Internal Family Systems. Useful if the inner critic feels like a separate voice.

books.title: The Body Keeps the Score
books.author: Bessel van der Kolk
books.why: Heavy, and widely over-recommended. Only if trauma is genuinely live for me.

books.title: Daring Greatly
books.author: Brené Brown
books.why: Vulnerability as strength rather than exposure. Relevant to a home where affection was, in my own word, "practical."

clusters.name: Meditation as a System
clusters.rationale: Technical, staged, falsifiable. No charisma, no personal brand, nothing being sold.

books.title: The Mind Illuminated
books.author: Culadasa (John Yates)
books.why: Ten stages with clear diagnostics and troubleshooting. Engineering-grade precision — the best meditation manual for a mind like mine.

books.title: Mindfulness in Plain English
books.author: Bhante Gunaratana
books.why: Free online, in full. No mysticism, no theatre, no teacher to trust.

books.title: Why Buddhism Is True
books.author: Robert Wright
books.why: Evolutionary psychology meets meditation. No faith required at any point.

books.title: Waking Up
books.author: Sam Harris
books.why: Contemplative practice with zero metaphysical claims attached.

books.title: 10% Happier
books.author: Dan Harris
books.why: A skeptic's memoir. Read only if I need permission before beginning.

clusters.name: Sleep & Circadian Rhythm
clusters.rationale: The 4:30–5:00am wake I want is only sustainable if this side is solved first.

books.title: Why We Sleep
books.author: Matthew Walker
books.why: The best single case for sleep as the foundation of everything else.

books.title: The Circadian Code
books.author: Satchin Panda
books.why: Light timing and eating windows, from a circadian researcher. Reference-grade.

books.title: Bigger Leaner Stronger
books.author: Michael Matthews
books.why: One complete, evidence-based program for a male lifter. Follow it and stop reading about training — the reading is the procrastination.

books.title: Built to Move
books.author: Kelly & Juliet Starrett
books.why: Ten mobility tests and the work to pass them. Directly serves "posture as confidence" and desk damage.

books.title: Starting Strength
books.author: Mark Rippetoe
books.why: Technique reference for the main barbell lifts. Consult chapters; don't read it through.

books.title: Endure
books.author: Alex Hutchinson
books.why: Where physical limits actually come from — mostly the brain. Good if my stamina concern is real.

clusters.name: Nutrition, Fasting & Longevity
clusters.rationale: 💡 *Context note: nearly all nutrition books assume a Western food environment. Dal-bhat, seasonal Nepali produce, and a South Asian metabolic profile all change the specifics. Take the principles — protein sufficiency, fibre, whole foods, meal timing — and rebuild the plan locally.

books.title: Outlive
books.author: Peter Attia
books.why: Healthspan over lifespan. The serious version of my "longevity mindset" — a framework and a set of markers, not a diet.

books.title: The Hungry Brain
books.author: Stephan Guyenet
books.why: Why eating goes wrong at the brain level. Removes moral judgement from food, which matters given how I talk to myself.

books.title: The Complete Guide to Fasting
books.author: Jason Fung
books.why: "Fasting protocols" from my hierarchy, with the physiology. Fung is a nephrologist with strong views; read the mechanism, hold the certainty loosely.

books.title: Breath
books.author: James Nestor
books.why: Excellent and genuinely useful on nasal breathing, CO₂ tolerance and slow breathing. Some historical and physiological claims are stretched for narrative effect — take the practices, hold the story loosely.

books.title: The Oxygen Advantage
books.author: Patrick McKeown
books.why: More rigorous, less readable. The technical companion to Nestor.

books.title: Burnout
books.author: Emily & Amelia Nagoski
books.why: "Completing the stress cycle" — the mechanism nearly every productivity book skips. Removing the stressor is not the same as discharging the stress.

books.title: Light on Pranayama
books.author: B.K.S. Iyengar
books.why: My hierarchy names pranayama specifically. This is the primary source, not a modern repackaging of it.

clusters.name: Yoga as Awareness
clusters.rationale: My hierarchy says "yoga as awareness, not fitness." These are the books that treat it that way.

books.title: Light on Yoga
books.author: B.K.S. Iyengar
books.why: The standard reference. Asana with precision and sequencing.

books.title: The Heart of Yoga
books.author: T.K.V. Desikachar
books.why: Yoga adapted to the person, not the person to the yoga. The philosophy that separates practice from performance.

books.title: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali
books.why: The philosophical root under all of it. Four short books of aphorisms; a lifetime of commentary.

domains.name: THINKING, LEARNING & DECISIONS
domains.question: Can I get genuinely good at things?

clusters.name: How to Actually Learn
clusters.rationale: The direct fix for my own sentence: "I mostly never go in depth, but shallow-learn everything quickly."

books.title: Ultralearning
books.author: Scott Young
books.why: Aggressive, project-based depth on a deadline. Nine principles, built around going absurdly deep on one thing instead of thinly across ten.

books.title: Make It Stick
books.author: Brown, Roediger & McDaniel
books.why: Why rereading and highlighting feel productive and don't work. Retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving. This will measurably improve my AI reading pipeline — especially the comprehension-check stage.

books.title: Peak
books.author: Anders Ericsson
books.why: Deliberate practice from the researcher whose work was mangled into the "10,000-hour rule." The real version is more demanding and more useful.

books.title: A Mind for Numbers
books.author: Barbara Oakley
books.why: Focused vs. diffuse mode. Useful concept, thin book.

books.title: Thinking in Systems
books.author: Donella Meadows
books.why: Stocks, flows, feedback loops, leverage points. My hierarchy says "systems thinking" five times without ever defining it. This defines it — and it will change how I read my own life document.

books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
books.author: Daniel Kahneman
books.why: Foundational on cognitive bias. The priming and social-priming chapters did not replicate, and Kahneman publicly acknowledged that section was built on too-weak evidence. The System 1/System 2 frame and the prospect-theory work stand.

books.title: The Great Mental Models, Vol. 1
books.author: Shane Parrish
books.why: Compact and well-chosen. One model per session.

books.title: Poor Charlie's Almanack
books.author: Charlie Munger
books.why: The multidisciplinary latticework, plus the psychology-of-misjudgement talk. Browse; don't march.

clusters.name: Deciding Under Uncertainty
clusters.rationale: Built specifically for an over-researcher who wants certainty before acting.

books.title: Thinking in Bets
books.author: Annie Duke
books.why: Separates decision quality from outcome quality. This single distinction is what lets a perfectionist act without a guaranteed result — the highest-leverage idea in this domain for me.

books.title: How to Decide
books.author: Annie Duke
books.why: The workbook version. Actual usable tools.

books.title: Decisive
books.author: Chip & Dan Heath
books.why: The WRAP framework. Practical and immediately applicable.

books.title: Superforecasting
books.author: Philip Tetlock
books.why: Calibrated prediction from a twenty-year forecasting tournament. Fascinating; less directly applicable.

books.title: How to Take Smart Notes
books.author: Sönke Ahrens
books.why: The Zettelkasten method. This turns my AI pipeline's chapter summaries from dead notes into a compounding asset — which is the difference between reading 100 books and having read 100 books.

books.title: On Writing Well
books.author: William Zinsser
books.why: Clear writing is clear thinking. Also feeds the Level 12 ambition to write.

books.title: Building a Second Brain
books.author: Tiago Forte
books.why: Capture, organise, distil, express. More app-centric than Ahrens; pick one, not both.

books.title: How to Read a Book
books.author: Adler & Van Doren
books.why: Four levels of reading — including inspectional reading, which is permission to extract a book's argument without finishing it. That permission is the missing piece in my current system.

books.title: Range
books.author: David Epstein
books.why: The evidenced case for generalists in complex domains. My own self-description — "hybrid: knowledge of various domains, able to go in depth on any" — with research behind it.

books.title: The Art of Learning
books.author: Josh Waitzkin
books.why: Chess prodigy to world champion in a martial art. Learning as a portable skill, told as memoir.

books.title: Curious
books.author: Ian Leslie
books.why: Curiosity as a maintainable habit rather than a fixed personality trait.

domains.name: CHARACTER, INTEGRITY & IDENTITY
domains.question: Who am I when it costs me something?

books.title: The Road to Character
books.author: David Brooks
books.why: Résumé virtues vs. eulogy virtues, illustrated through eight lives. The distinction my Level 2 is circling without naming.

books.title: Nicomachean Ethics
books.author: Aristotle
books.why: "Aristotle's virtue ethics" from my hierarchy. Excellence as habit, not as event — and the doctrine of the mean, which is the classical argument against perfectionism.

books.title: The Second Mountain
books.author: David Brooks
books.why: From achievement to commitment. The transition I'll face in my thirties, described in advance.

books.title: After Virtue
books.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
books.why: Academic and difficult. Why modern moral language fragmented. Only if 5.1 genuinely grips me.

books.title: Lying
books.author: Sam Harris
books.why: A 60-page essay arguing that even small, kind lies cost more than they save. Aimed squarely at the gap I named about myself: "I am not a very truthful person, sometimes manipulative," alongside "manipulating people to get benefits is what makes me lose respect for myself." Those two sentences cannot both stand.

books.title: The Speed of Trust
books.author: Stephen M.R. Covey
books.why: Trust as a measurable economic asset with a dividend and a tax. Bridges character into career.

books.title: Integrity
books.author: Stephen L. Carter
books.why: Discern what's right, act on it, say so openly. The three-part definition, argued carefully.

books.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
books.author: Stephen Covey
books.why: Character ethic over personality ethic. Written in 1989 and still nearly my Level 2 verbatim. Dated in tone; sound in structure.

books.title: Immunity to Change
books.author: Kegan & Lahey
books.why: Why sincere resolutions fail — because a competing hidden commitment is protecting me from something. This explains my procrastination more precisely than any discipline book on this list.

books.title: Transitions
books.author: William Bridges
books.why: Ending, neutral zone, new beginning. Navigating identity between life phases.

books.title: The Courage to Be Disliked
books.author: Kishimi & Koga
books.why: "Courage to be disliked" is already listed as a value in my hierarchy. This is its source: Adlerian psychology in Socratic dialogue, and the sharpest available argument against organising a life around external validation.

books.title: The Obstacle Is the Way
books.author: Ryan Holiday
books.why: Applied Stoicism in modern packaging. Thin compared to the originals, but it travels well on a hard day.

books.title: Antifragile
books.author: Nassim Taleb
books.why: Gaining from disorder rather than merely surviving it. Arrogant in tone, genuinely original in substance.

clusters.name: Service Without Martyrdom
clusters.rationale: Saying "no" rated **3/10**. Default tendency: **over-give**. Responsible for everyone else's work but not my own. This cluster is the correction.

books.title: Give and Take
books.author: Adam Grant
books.why: Givers occupy both the top and the bottom of every success distribution. The variable is whether they are "otherish" or purely selfless. That single distinction is the thing I'm missing.

books.title: The Art of Possibility
books.author: Zander & Zander
books.why: Contribution as a stance rather than a sacrifice. Written by a conductor and a therapist; unusual and warm.

books.title: Nonviolent Communication
books.author: Marshall Rosenberg
books.why: Observation → feeling → need → request. The highest-leverage communication framework available, and it works through honesty rather than technique — which is the only version I'd be able to use without losing self-respect.

books.title: Crucial Conversations
books.author: Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler
books.why: For exactly the moments I described: "I initially feel extremely sad, and explain later." This is how to explain earlier, while it still matters.

books.title: Difficult Conversations
books.author: Stone, Patton & Heen
books.why: From the Harvard Negotiation Project. The "what happened / feelings / identity" three-conversation model is the deepest cut here.

books.title: Supercommunicators
books.author: Charles Duhigg
books.why: Recent, readable, built on matching the type of conversation the other person is actually having.

books.title: You're Not Listening
books.author: Kate Murphy
books.why: Sharpens the one skill I already have naturally. Confirmation plus refinement.

books.title: Set Boundaries, Find Peace
books.author: Nedra Glover Tawwab
books.why: Practical, scripted, unsentimental. Written for precisely a 3/10 no-sayer who over-gives and then resents it.

books.title: Not Nice
books.author: Aziz Gazipura
books.why: Long and repetitive, and still the best book on people-pleasing specifically. Skim aggressively; the exercises are the value.

books.title: The Book of Boundaries
books.author: Melissa Urban
books.why: Ready-made scripts sorted by relationship type. A lookup table for when the words won't come.

clusters.name: Family, Parents & Generational Patterns
clusters.rationale: I feel gratitude toward my family and rate them 10/10. This cluster isn't about revising that. It's about understanding a home where affection was, in my own word, "practical" — and where I've since noticed a deep desire for open affection.

books.title: It Didn't Start with You
books.author: Mark Wolynn
books.why: "Generational healing" is my own phrase. This is that topic, done readably, with concrete exercises.

books.title: The Dance of Connection
books.author: Harriet Lerner
books.why: Changing my part in a family pattern without needing a confrontation or anyone else's agreement.

books.title: Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents
books.author: Lindsay Gibson
books.why: Only if the "practical affection" note keeps resurfacing on its own. If chapter one doesn't resonate, close it — this is not a box to tick.

clusters.name: Fatherhood & Raising Children
clusters.rationale: My hierarchy has a full Children section: role modeling, setting example by actions, teaching, empowering. Mapped now, read when relevant.

books.title: How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk
books.author: Faber & Mazlish
books.why: The most practical parenting book written. Scripts and cartoons, not theory. Still the standard after forty years.

books.title: The Whole-Brain Child
books.author: Siegel & Bryson
books.why: Twelve strategies grounded in child brain development. Short and immediately usable.

books.title: Hunt, Gather, Parent
books.author: Michaeleen Doucleff
books.why: Maya, Inuit and Hadzabe parenting practices. A useful counterweight to Western intensive parenting — though it romanticises at points.

books.title: The Gardener and the Carpenter
books.author: Alison Gopnik
books.why: A developmental psychologist arguing against parenting-as-optimization. **Read this one before I over-engineer a childhood** — it is the direct antidote to applying "perfect in everything" to a child.

clusters.name: Friendship & Social Capacity for an Introvert

books.title: Quiet
books.author: Susan Cain
books.why: Introversion as an asset with its own physiology, not a defect to be corrected. I listed being an introvert alongside my problems. It isn't one.
books.clusterName: Friendship & Social Capacity for an Introvert

books.title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
books.author: Dale Carnegie
books.why: 1936, and still unbeaten. Converts the listening I already do naturally into warmth people actually remember.
books.clusterName: Friendship & Social Capacity for an Introvert

books.title: Platonic
books.author: Marisa Franco
books.why: Adult friendship through attachment theory. Directly addresses my own line: "when friendships fade, I feel loss and try to revive."
books.clusterName: Friendship & Social Capacity for an Introvert

books.title: The Art of Gathering
books.author: Priya Parker
books.why: Hosting my small circle with intention. Practical for someone who wants few, deep bonds rather than many light ones.
books.clusterName: Friendship & Social Capacity for an Introvert

domains.name: LOVE, ATTRACTION & PARTNERSHIP
domains.question: Who do I build a life with?

clusters.name: Love as a Capacity, Not a Search
clusters.rationale: Read this cluster **before** 7.3.

books.title: The Art of Loving
books.author: Erich Fromm
books.why: 120 pages, 1956, still unbeaten. Its central argument: the problem is almost never finding the right person to love — it's developing the capacity to love, which is a discipline like any other. Written for the exact belief I'm currently holding.
books.clusterName: Love as a Capacity, Not a Search

books.title: The Course of Love
books.author: Alain de Botton
books.why: A novel that follows one marriage across twenty years, with philosophical commentary threaded through. It dismantles Romanticism — the belief that the right person means no work. Reads as fiction, lands as instruction.
books.clusterName: Love as a Capacity, Not a Search

books.title: Essays in Love
books.author: Alain de Botton
books.why: de Botton's earlier, funnier version. One relationship from first glance to end, narrated with footnotes.
books.clusterName: Love as a Capacity, Not a Search

books.title: Attached
books.author: Levine & Heller
books.why: Anxious, avoidant, secure. I wrote "attach slowly, selectively" and then answered "don't know" to both "what do you feel when someone gets close" and "emotional vulnerability comfort, 1–10." This book answers both in one chapter and reframes everything after it.

books.title: Hold Me Tight
books.author: Sue Johnson
books.why: Emotionally Focused Therapy. The chapters on recurring conflict cycles are the useful part.

clusters.name: Meeting People & Dating Honestly
clusters.rationale: 💡 **An honest gap.** Every book in this cluster assumes a Western dating market — apps, serial dating, individual choice. Kathmandu, family expectation, and the reality that arranged and semi-arranged introductions are still normal in Nepal change the mechanics substantially. **The psychology transfers; the logistics don't.** No book on this list solves that, and I shouldn't pretend one does. What transfers is: knowing my attachment pattern, knowing that "perfect" is a trap, and knowing what predicts a lasting partnership. How I meet someone is a local question, and family conversations are part of it.

books.title: How to Not Die Alone
books.author: Logan Ury
books.why: A behavioural scientist turned dating coach. Contains a chapter specifically on the **Maximizer** — the person searching for the perfect partner and therefore never choosing. That chapter is written about me. Start there, not at page one.

books.title: The Defining Decade
books.author: Meg Jay
books.why: I am 25. This is the book on why 25–35 compounds more than any other decade — across work, identity, and relationships — and it is only useful while it's still true.

books.title: Models: Attract Women Through Honesty
books.author: Mark Manson
books.why: The one book in this genre built on non-neediness and honest self-presentation rather than routines. Included precisely because its whole argument is against the manipulation approach.

books.title: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
books.author: John Gottman
books.why: Four decades of longitudinal observation on what actually predicts whether couples last. The Four Horsemen, bids for connection, repair attempts. Measurement, not opinion — which is the only register I'll fully trust here.

books.title: The All-or-Nothing Marriage
books.author: Eli Finkel
books.why: Why modern expectations of a single partner are historically unprecedented. Read it to calibrate what the word "perfect" could even mean.

books.title: Eight Dates
books.author: John & Julie Gottman
books.why: Eight structured conversations every couple should have. A practical companion, not a standalone.

clusters.name: Desire, Intimacy & Sexuality
clusters.rationale: My hierarchy lists "sex, desires, fantasy, spiciness." Treated here as adult education with a factual basis, not as mystique and not as conquest.

books.title: Mating in Captivity
books.author: Esther Perel
books.why: The tension between security and desire — that the conditions for one often undermine the other. The serious treatment of the "polarity balance" my hierarchy names.

books.title: Come As You Are
books.author: Emily Nagoski
books.why: A sex educator on responsive desire, context, and the dual control model. Written about women's sexuality, and the single highest-value thing a man can read on the subject.

books.title: She Comes First
books.author: Ian Kerner
books.why: Practical and clinical. Partner-focused rather than performance-focused.

books.title: So Good They Can't Ignore You
books.author: Cal Newport
books.why: "Follow your passion" is bad advice; build rare and valuable career capital, then trade it for autonomy. The strategic foundation for the whole domain — and a direct argument against shallow-learning everything.

books.title: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
books.author: Eric Jorgenson
books.why: Free in full online. Leverage, specific knowledge, judgement, equity over salary. Short, dense, rereadable, and the cleanest bridge from career into wealth.

books.title: The Staff Engineer's Path
books.author: Tanya Reilly
books.why: Technical influence without a title — my hierarchy's exact phrase — if I take the senior-IC route before management.

books.title: Designing Your Life
books.author: Burnett & Evans
books.why: Stanford design thinking applied to a career. Light on theory, strong on exercises. Also serves Domain 1.6.

books.title: The Manager's Path
books.author: Camille Fournier
books.why: Written by a former CTO and structured exactly as the ladder: mentee → mentor → tech lead → manager → director → VP/CTO. If CTO is the ten-year goal, this is the map. Read it well before I need it.

books.title: High Output Management
books.author: Andy Grove
books.why: Managerial leverage, from Intel's CEO. Fifty years old and still the sharpest thing written on the subject.

books.title: An Elegant Puzzle
books.author: Will Larson
books.why: Systems thinking applied to engineering organisations. Pairs directly with Fournier.

books.title: The Making of a Manager
books.author: Julie Zhuo
books.why: The honest first-year-manager account. A gentler entry point than Grove.

books.title: Team Topologies
books.author: Skelton & Pais
books.why: Org design as system design. Reference when I'm actually structuring teams.

books.title: Accelerate
books.author: Forsgren, Humble & Kim
books.why: What actually predicts engineering performance, from multi-year survey research. Data instead of opinion — useful ammunition in any technical-leadership argument.

clusters.name: Leading Without Ego
clusters.rationale: "Calm leader," "silent authority," "leadership without ego theatrics" — my own words. These are the books for that exact style, not for the loud version.

books.title: Radical Candor
books.author: Kim Scott
books.why: Care personally **and** challenge directly. That is literally my two stated values — kindness and honesty — turned into a management framework. It also names my likely failure mode by name: **ruinous empathy**, which is exactly where a 3/10 no-sayer ends up.

books.title: Turn the Ship Around!
books.author: David Marquet
books.why: A submarine captain replaces command-and-control with intent-based leadership. The best available working model of quiet authority.

books.title: Multipliers
books.author: Liz Wiseman
books.why: Leaders who make everyone around them smarter, vs. those who drain. My "empowering" instinct, systematised and measurable.

books.title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
books.author: Patrick Lencioni
books.why: Fable format. Two hours, one durable pyramid.

books.title: Leaders Eat Last
books.author: Simon Sinek
books.why: Psychological safety as the basis of trust. Repetitive, but the core idea is sound.

clusters.name: Negotiation, Power & Self-Advocacy
clusters.rationale: My named blind spot, in my own words: responsible for others' work — office, friends, clubs — but not at a personal level.

books.title: Never Split the Difference
books.author: Chris Voss
books.why: Tactical empathy, calibrated questions, mirroring, labelling. It works **because** I'm a natural listener — it's the rare negotiation approach that plays to introversion. The most immediately usable book in this domain: salary, scope, deadlines, vendors, family.

books.title: Getting to Yes
books.author: Fisher & Ury
books.why: Principled, interests-based negotiation. The ethical foundation sitting underneath Voss's tactics.

books.title: The Laws of Human Nature
books.author: Robert Greene
books.why: Read defensively — to recognise what is being done to me, never as a playbook. Greene's earlier* 48 Laws of Power *is deliberately excluded; see the exclusions list.

books.title: Mastery
books.author: Robert Greene
books.why: The apprenticeship arc drawn from real lives. Greene at his most constructive.

books.title: Shop Class as Soulcraft
books.author: Matthew Crawford
books.why: A philosopher who became a motorcycle mechanic, on the dignity and cognition of skilled work.

books.title: The Craftsman
books.author: Richard Sennett
books.why: "Craftsmanship pride" from my hierarchy, treated academically and at length.

crossRefs.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance

clusters.name: Technology, AI & the Decade I'll Build In
clusters.rationale: *New cluster.** *My baseline says my professional identity is "software engineering / AI / future skills, dynamic mastery" and that I want to be proactive about "future market needs." None of that is served by coding manuals — which I excluded, correctly. It's served by understanding where the industry is going. These are strategy and economics books that happen to be about technology.

books.title: The Coming Wave
books.author: Mustafa Suleyman
books.why: DeepMind co-founder on AI and synthetic biology as containment problems. The most serious mainstream book on what the next decade actually looks like from inside the industry.
books.clusterName: Technology, AI & the Decade I'll Build In

books.title: Co-Intelligence
books.author: Ethan Mollick
books.why: A Wharton professor on working with AI as a collaborator. Immediately practical — and directly relevant, since my entire reading system is built on an AI pipeline. This will make that pipeline better.
books.clusterName: Technology, AI & the Decade I'll Build In

books.title: Chip War
books.author: Chris Miller
books.why: How semiconductors became the choke point of the world economy. Explains the single supply chain that most determines my industry's future and Asia's position in it.
books.clusterName: Technology, AI & the Decade I'll Build In

books.title: AI 2041
books.author: Kai-Fu Lee & Chen Qiufan
books.why: Ten near-future stories, each followed by technical analysis. Includes scenarios set in South Asia — rare, and relevant to where I'll be building.
books.clusterName: Technology, AI & the Decade I'll Build In

books.title: Power and Prediction
books.author: Agrawal, Gans & Goldfarb
books.why: AI as a drop in the cost of prediction, and why system-level redesign captures the value rather than point solutions. The economist's frame — useful for a founder deciding what to build.
books.clusterName: Technology, AI & the Decade I'll Build In

books.title: The Mom Test
books.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
books.why: ~130 pages on how to talk to customers so they tell you the truth instead of being polite. One evening; prevents years of building the wrong thing. **Start the entire domain here.**

books.title: Zero to One
books.author: Peter Thiel
books.why: Monopoly over competition, secrets, the contrarian question. Short, opinionated, genuinely clarifying about what a business is for.

books.title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
books.author: Ben Horowitz
books.why: The unglamorous reality of running a company in trouble. Essential calibration against founder mythology.

books.title: The Lean Startup
books.author: Eric Ries
books.why: Historically important, now largely absorbed into standard practice. Skim the MVP and validated-learning chapters.

clusters.name: Selling & Distribution
clusters.rationale: The engineer's largest gap, without exception — and mine, given that I'm an introvert who dislikes crowds.

books.title: To Sell Is Human
books.author: Daniel Pink
books.why: Reframes selling as moving people, with attunement and buoyancy as learnable skills. **Read this before any tactical sales book**, or I'll reject the entire subject as beneath me.

books.title: Obviously Awesome
books.author: April Dunford
books.why: Positioning, in about 150 pages. The missing skill behind most technically-excellent failed products.

books.title: $100M Offers
books.author: Alex Hormozi
books.why: Self-promotional in tone; the offer-construction framework underneath is genuinely good. Take the framework, ignore the persona.

books.title: Traction
books.author: Weinberg & Mares
books.why: Nineteen distribution channels, tested systematically. Open when I have something to distribute.

books.title: Inspired
books.author: Marty Cagan
books.why: How strong product teams actually operate. The reference on product management.

books.title: Hooked
books.author: Nir Eyal
books.why: Habit-forming product design. Read with the ethics question deliberately open — this is the mechanism behind the apps in Domain 1.3.

books.title: Shape Up
books.author: Ryan Singer
books.why: Free online. Six-week cycles, appetite instead of estimates. Short and directly usable in engineering work.

clusters.name: Systems, Delegation & Stepping Out
clusters.rationale: "Knowing when to stop and leave for system" — my own words. And: "a system and family business system where all family works within the system is ideal." I already have the instinct. This is the method.

books.title: The E-Myth Revisited
books.author: Michael Gerber
books.why: Work **on** the business, not **in** it. Build it as if you'll franchise it. This is precisely my family-business-system idea, written out as a method — including why most family businesses fail at exactly the point I'm describing. Read it when a venture is real, not before.

books.title: Buy Back Your Time
books.author: Dan Martell
books.why: Delegation mechanics for founders who won't let go. Practical and modern.

books.title: Built to Sell
books.author: John Warrillow
books.why: A business that runs without me. The exit-oriented version of Gerber.

books.title: Company of One
books.author: Paul Jarvis
books.why: The counterweight: staying small on purpose. Worth reading purely to test whether scale is what I actually want, or what I've assumed I should want.

books.title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy
books.author: Richard Rumelt
books.why: Most "strategy" is ambition with slides. This teaches the difference — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — and it's immediately useful inside my day job, not just in a future company.

books.title: 7 Powers
books.author: Hamilton Helmer
books.why: Seven sources of durable competitive advantage. Dense, short, unusually rigorous.

books.title: The Personal MBA
books.author: Josh Kaufman
books.why: Broad business literacy in one volume. Suits my generalist instinct. Browse by chapter; never read straight through.

clusters.name: Money Psychology
clusters.rationale: Start here. I already know I overspend — I wrote it down myself. The gap is not information.

books.title: The Psychology of Money
books.author: Morgan Housel
books.why: Nineteen short, independent chapters on why financial behaviour beats financial knowledge. The correct first book for someone whose problem is behavioural, not analytical.

books.title: Your Money or Your Life
books.author: Robin & Dominguez
books.why: Money as life energy traded for hours. It changes how I evaluate both a purchase and a job offer, permanently.

books.title: Die With Zero
books.author: Bill Perkins
books.why: The counterweight to pure accumulation. Fits my own line — "why not live life to the fullest" — by arguing that the timing of experiences matters as much as the saving.

books.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
books.author: George Clason
books.why: ~100 pages of parables. Pay yourself first, make gold work, guard against loss. No market-specific advice to translate — universally applicable, readable in a weekend.

books.title: The Millionaire Next Door
books.author: Stanley & Danko
books.why: Wealth is what you don't spend. Aimed squarely at lifestyle inflation, which I named as my own weakness. Note: the underlying survey data is from 1990s America — the behavioural finding travels, the specific figures don't.

books.title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
books.author: Ramit Sethi
books.why: Excellent automation philosophy attached to heavily US-specific accounts. Take the system, replace every product.

books.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
books.author: John Bogle
books.why: Low-cost index investing, argued simply by the man who invented the index fund. The default that beats most active strategies — including any I'd design. Adapt the vehicle to what exists in Nepal.

books.title: A Random Walk Down Wall Street
books.author: Burton Malkiel
books.why: The fuller academic case. Efficient markets, bubbles, asset allocation across a life.

books.title: The Intelligent Investor
books.author: Benjamin Graham
books.why: Chapters 8 (Mr. Market) and 20 (margin of safety) are the famous ones. Read those; treat the rest as reference.

books.title: One Up On Wall Street
books.author: Peter Lynch
books.why: Only if I ever pick individual stocks. After Bogle, never instead of.

books.title: Principles
books.author: Ray Dalio
books.why: Part 1 (Life) and Part 3 (Work) are the valuable sections. Long, repetitive, and worth skimming without guilt.

clusters.name: Macro, Systems & the Wider Board
clusters.rationale: "Understanding other factors affecting finances — politics, world economics, wars, policies." My hierarchy asked for this explicitly.

books.title: How Asia Works
books.author: Joe Studwell
books.why: Why some Asian economies developed and others didn't: land reform, export discipline, financial repression. The most useful economics book I can read as a Nepali who intends to build here — it explains what my country did and didn't do, and why.

books.title: The Changing World Order
books.author: Ray Dalio
books.why: Long-term debt cycles, reserve currencies, empires rising and falling. Exactly the frame my hierarchy describes wanting. Dalio's pattern-matching is bold; treat it as a lens, not a prophecy.

books.title: Poor Economics
books.author: Banerjee & Duflo
books.why: Nobel-winning randomised fieldwork on how poverty actually behaves. Directly relevant to South Asia and to any business serving low-income customers.

books.title: Debt: The First 5,000 Years
books.author: David Graeber
books.why: Anthropology of money and obligation. Slow, contested by some economists, and genuinely assumption-breaking.

clusters.name: Speaking & Presenting
clusters.rationale: 💡 **Not a book, and more important than the books:** reading about speaking does approximately nothing. Kathmandu has active Toastmasters clubs. **One book plus one club beats ten books.** For an introvert, the structured, low-stakes format is the point.

books.title: TED Talks
books.author: Chris Anderson
books.why: By the man who has curated and watched more talks than anyone alive. Throughline, structure, delivery, and what actually fails. Serves both public speaking and the Level 12 teaching ambition.

books.title: Confessions of a Public Speaker
books.author: Scott Berkun
books.why: Honest, funny, and deflating in the best way. Read it first if the fear is the blocker.

books.title: The Charisma Myth
books.author: Olivia Fox Cabane
books.why: Charisma as three learnable behaviours — presence, power, warmth — rather than a personality I either have or don't. Written with introverts explicitly in mind and full of drills.

books.title: Captivate
books.author: Vanessa Van Edwards
books.why: Tactical social science for someone who finds rooms genuinely draining. Useful scripts for the first five minutes.

books.title: Presence
books.author: Amy Cuddy
books.why: The power-posing finding failed replication, and Cuddy has publicly engaged with the criticism. The broader material on impostor feelings and self-doubt still holds. Read knowing which part is which.

clusters.name: Style, Fit & What Suits Me
clusters.rationale: My hierarchy asks, in my own words, for "deep study of what looks good on me — skin tone, body type." The honest answer: there is one real book, and almost everything else is noise, opinion, or advertising.

books.title: Dressing the Man
books.author: Alan Flusser
books.why: The definitive work on proportion, fit, and matching colour and contrast to my own skin tone and features. Its opening chapters are literally about determining what works for a specific person's colouring — it answers my question permanently, once. **At 165 cm, the chapters on proportion and tailoring matter more than any brand ever will.**

books.title: True Style
books.author: G. Bruce Boyer
books.why: The reasoning behind the rules, essay by essay. Shorter and more pleasurable than Flusser.

books.title: What Every BODY Is Saying
books.author: Joe Navarro
books.why: Ex-FBI, and the best of a weak genre — useful for becoming aware of my own posture and signalling.

clusters.name: Environment, Order & Aesthetics
clusters.rationale: "Order as self-respect." Structured, clean, cozy, managed — my own description of where I feel most like myself.

books.title: Goodbye, Things
books.author: Fumio Sasaki
books.why: Minimalism without the ideology or the smugness. Practical and calm.

books.title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up
books.author: Marie Kondo
books.why: One method, executed once, completely. Then stop reading about tidying — this is a domain where reading more is the failure mode.

books.title: In Praise of Shadows
books.author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
books.why: Eastern aesthetics in 70 pages: shadow, patina, imperfection. Closer to my own aesthetic inheritance than any Western design book, and a quiet argument against the perfect surface.

books.title: A Pattern Language
books.author: Christopher Alexander
books.why: 253 patterns for why some spaces feel alive and others don't. Deep, endlessly browsable, and secretly a systems-thinking book.

books.title: The Book of Delights
books.author: Ross Gay
books.why: A year of short daily essays, each about one small pleasure the author noticed on purpose. The best available training in a skill I do not currently have: noticing good things while they're happening rather than auditing them afterward.

books.title: Play
books.author: Stuart Brown
books.why: Play as biological necessity rather than indulgence. Permission, with evidence attached — which is the only form of permission I'll accept.

books.title: Wintering
books.author: Katherine May
books.why: Rest and retreat during fallow seasons. For the periods when the system isn't working and I'm about to blame myself for it.

clusters.name: Nature, Wilderness & Solitude
clusters.rationale: "Solitude in wilderness," "nature immersion" — my hierarchy — and "solitude, nature, self time" as my own stated recharge mode. This is not optional reading; it's the mechanism I already rely on.

books.title: The Comfort Crisis
books.author: Michael Easter
books.why: Discomfort, boredom, hunger and wilderness as inputs I've quietly engineered out of my life. Built around a 33-day Arctic hunt, with the research threaded through.

books.title: The Nature Fix
books.author: Florence Williams
books.why: The measured cognitive and physiological effects of time outdoors. Turns "go for a walk" into a dosed intervention.

books.title: Walden
books.author: Henry David Thoreau
books.why: Deliberate living, stripped to essentials. Free, slow on purpose, and best read a few pages at a time.

books.title: Wanderlust: A History of Walking
books.author: Rebecca Solnit
books.why: Walking as thinking, across philosophy, politics and pilgrimage.

clusters.name: Mountains & Himalaya
clusters.rationale: 🇳🇵 *Hiking and trekking are named in my hierarchy, and the Himalaya are outside my window. Very few people get to read great literature about their own landscape.

books.title: The Snow Leopard
books.author: Peter Matthiessen
books.why: A 1973 trek through Dolpo with the biologist George Schaller that becomes a book about grief, Zen practice, and not getting the thing you came for. National Book Award winner, and the finest book written about walking in Nepal.

books.title: Into Thin Air
books.author: Jon Krakauer
books.why: The 1996 Everest disaster, reported from inside it. Also a study in how ambition and summit-fever override judgement — read it that way.

books.title: Himalaya: A Human History
books.author: Ed Douglas
books.why: The range as a human place across millennia — empires, trade, religion, exploration — rather than as a backdrop for Western climbers.

books.title: Touching My Father's Soul
books.author: Jamling Tenzing Norgay
books.why: Everest from the Sherpa side, by Tenzing Norgay's son. The perspective the famous books leave out.

books.title: Annapurna
books.author: Maurice Herzog
books.why: The first 8,000m summit. Nepal, 1950. A period document as much as an account — read it with that in mind.

books.title: The Art of Travel
books.author: Alain de Botton
books.why: Why travel so often disappoints, and how to fix that before booking rather than after.

books.title: Vagabonding
books.author: Rolf Potts
books.why: Long-term travel as a design choice with a budget, not a fantasy.

books.title: The Songlines
books.author: Bruce Chatwin
books.why: Walking, myth and restlessness. Genre-blurring and beautiful.

books.title: How to Do Nothing
books.author: Jenny Odell
books.why: Attention as both a personal and a political act. Pairs hard with Domain 1.3 — and argues, usefully, that the goal isn't more productive attention but attention returned to me.

books.title: In Praise of Slowness
books.author: Carl Honoré
books.why: The case against speed as a default setting.

books.title: The Art of Simple Living
books.author: Shunmyō Masuno
books.why: 100 short Zen practices, one page each. A Buddhist priest and garden designer. Ideal for a two-minute morning read.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: Marcus Aurelius
books.why: A Roman emperor's private notebook, never intended for publication — which is precisely why it's trustworthy. A few pages at a time, for years. The ideal slow companion for my temperament.

books.title: Letters from a Stoic
books.author: Seneca
books.why: Warmer and more practical than Marcus. Read as individual letters, never as a book.

books.title: Discourses and Selected Writings
books.author: Epictetus
books.why: The dichotomy of control at its source, from a former slave. Free in older translations.

books.title: The Practicing Stoic
books.author: Ward Farnsworth
books.why: Organised by theme, with the original passages alongside. The best single reference for the school.

books.title: A Guide to the Good Life
books.author: William Irvine
books.why: A modern systematic introduction, for when I want the framework before the fragments.

books.title: Man's Search for Meaning
books.author: Viktor Frankl
books.why: A psychiatrist's account of the camps, and the argument that meaning is found rather than given, and survives conditions that destroy everything else. Short and permanently altering. Serves my Level 1 work on suffering and death directly.

books.title: The Myth of Sisyphus
books.author: Albert Camus
books.why: "Camus' absurd courage" is in my hierarchy. This is the source. Read the first essay and the final pages; the middle is literary criticism.

books.title: When Breath Becomes Air
books.author: Paul Kalanithi
books.why: A neurosurgeon's memoir of dying at 37. My hierarchy lists "death contemplation" as a practice; this makes it real rather than theoretical.

books.title: Being Mortal
books.author: Atul Gawande
books.why: Aging, medicine, and what a good ending actually requires. Practical as well as philosophical — and relevant to my parents, not only to me.

books.title: The Denial of Death
books.author: Ernest Becker
books.why: Pulitzer winner. How mortality-denial quietly drives ambition, culture and the need to be exceptional. Heavy, and uncomfortably close to "perfect in everything."

books.title: The Bhagavad Gita
books.why: Action without attachment to fruit, dharma, duty — the exact concepts sitting in my Level 1. Easwaran's introduction and chapter prefaces make it genuinely readable without diluting it.

books.title: The Upanishads
books.why: The philosophical root beneath the Gita. Older, stranger, less prescriptive.

books.title: Vivekachudamani / Self-Knowledge
books.author: Adi Shankaracharya
books.why: I named Shankaracharya myself as someone I don't know enough about. Unassisted Shankara is hard going — use a commentaried edition, not a bare translation.

books.title: I Am That
books.author: Nisargadatta Maharaj
books.why: Dialogues. Direct, uncompromising, no method offered. Not a first book.

books.title: The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are
books.author: Alan Watts
books.why: A clear Western entry point to non-duality. An explainer, not a substitute for the sources.

clusters.name: Buddhism & Newar Heritage
clusters.rationale: 🇳🇵 *My own inheritance. The Kathmandu Valley preserved a living Mahayana and Vajrayana tradition after Buddhism had largely disappeared from the rest of South Asia — which makes Newar Buddhism genuinely unusual, and almost entirely unknown to the people who grew up inside it.

books.title: What the Buddha Taught
books.author: Walpola Rahula
books.why: The clearest concise presentation of core Buddhism, by a monk-scholar. No mysticism, no salesmanship, no teacher to trust — just the four truths, the eightfold path, and the texts.

books.title: The Dhammapada
books.why: Verses. A handful at a time, indefinitely.

books.title: Old Path White Clouds
books.author: Thich Nhat Hanh
books.why: The Buddha's life told as narrative, drawn from the Pali texts. Gentle, long, and it reads like fiction.

books.title: Monk, Householder, and Tantric Priest
books.author: David N. Gellner
books.why: A rigorous ethnography of Newar Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism, based on fieldwork in Lalitpur. Academic and dense — and it is the serious scholarly study of my own tradition. Very few people ever read a book of this calibre about their own culture.

books.title: Rebuilding Buddhism
books.author: Sarah LeVine & David N. Gellner
books.why: The twentieth-century Theravada revival movement in Nepal — how it grew, who resisted it, and what it changed. The modern half of the story Gellner's earlier book tells.

books.title: Freedom from the Known
books.author: J. Krishnamurti
books.why: I named him myself. He spent his life dissolving the organisation built around him and telling people to accept no authority, including his own. The right teacher for a skeptic — and the hardest, because he offers no method, no stages, and nothing to be perfect at.

books.title: Think on These Things
books.author: J. Krishnamurti
books.why: Talks given to students. More accessible, more concrete.

books.title: The First and Last Freedom
books.author: J. Krishnamurti
books.why: With Aldous Huxley's introduction, which is the best short summary of Krishnamurti's position anyone has written.

clusters.name: Taoism & Effortless Action
clusters.rationale: "Taoist flow" is in my hierarchy — and this is the most direct counterweight in the entire document to my instinct to force, grip, and optimise.

books.title: Tao Te Ching
books.edition: Stephen Mitchell or D.C. Lau translation
books.why: 81 short chapters. Reread for life. The single strongest argument against the belief that trying harder is always the answer.

books.title: The Way of Chuang Tzu
books.author: Thomas Merton
books.why: A Trappist monk's renderings of Chuang Tzu. Playful, strange, and deeper than it looks.

books.title: Trying Not to Try
books.author: Edward Slingerland
books.why: Wu wei explained through cognitive science — the paradox that some things can only be achieved by not aiming at them. Written for people who need the mechanism before they'll accept the idea. That's me.

clusters.name: Telling Real from Fraudulent
clusters.rationale: I already have this instinct. This cluster turns instinct into a tool I can state out loud.

books.title: The Demon-Haunted World
books.author: Carl Sagan
books.why: The "baloney detection kit" chapter alone justifies the book. A permanent, portable filter for every guru, course, supplement and certainty I will ever be sold — including the ones I'd want to believe.

books.title: The Guru Papers
books.author: Kramer & Alstad
books.why: The structural mechanics of authoritarian spirituality: why the pattern repeats across traditions, and how surrender gets converted into control.

books.title: Sophie's World
books.author: Jostein Gaarder
books.why: The entire history of Western philosophy as a novel, written for a fourteen-year-old. The most painless entry that exists, and not a dumbed-down one.

books.title: The Problems of Philosophy
books.author: Bertrand Russell
books.why: Short, rigorous, clear. Free. The best hundred pages on what philosophy actually asks.

books.title: Beyond Good and Evil
books.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
books.why: "Nietzsche's self-overcoming" is in my hierarchy. Difficult and easily misread — read with a companion text, not alone.

books.title: Existentialism Is a Humanism
books.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
books.why: One lecture. Radical freedom and total responsibility, with nowhere to hide.

books.title: On Writing
books.author: Stephen King
books.why: Half memoir, half craft manual, entirely honest. The best book on writing prose, and short enough to finish in a week.

books.title: Bird by Bird
books.author: Anne Lamott
books.why: Permission to write badly first. The chapter on shitty first drafts is aimed directly at perfectionism, and is arguably the most useful three pages in this domain for me specifically.

books.title: Show Your Work
books.author: Austin Kleon
books.why: Sharing process rather than only finished results. The antidote to waiting until something is perfect before anyone sees it.

books.title: Steal Like an Artist
books.author: Austin Kleon
books.why: One hour. Creative permission, illustrated.

books.title: The Coaching Habit
books.author: Michael Bungay Stanier
books.why: Seven questions, and the discipline to ask rather than advise. Built for exactly my profile: a natural listener with mentor energy and a strong urge to solve other people's problems for them.

books.title: Co-Active Coaching
books.author: Kimsey-House et al.
books.why: The professional framework, if the Level 12 coaching ambition ever becomes real.

books.title: The Art of Explanation
books.author: Lee LeFever
books.why: Making complex things simple for people who don't share my context. Underrated for a technical person who wants to teach.

books.title: Get Together
books.author: Richardson, Huynh & Bailey
books.why: How communities actually start — with a few people doing something, not with a platform. Practical and short.

books.title: Community: The Structure of Belonging
books.author: Peter Block
books.why: The deeper theory. Slower, more abstract, more durable.

books.title: Doing Good Better
books.author: William MacAskill
books.why: Effective altruism: how to make giving actually count rather than merely feel good. Directly serves the "social service" pull I named without knowing what to do with it.

books.title: Let My People Go Surfing
books.author: Yvon Chouinard
books.why: Patagonia, built as a values statement, and profitable anyway. The proof case for "ethical monetization" and "wealth creation as service."

books.title: Building a StoryBrand
books.author: Donald Miller
books.why: Clarifying a message so that people act on it. Mechanical, and it works.

books.title: Perennial Seller
books.author: Ryan Holiday
books.why: Making work that lasts rather than work that trends. The right frame for someone thinking in decades.

domains.name: STORY, LITERATURE & LIVES
domains.question: What can't be argued, only shown?

books.title: Siddhartha
books.author: Hermann Hesse
books.why: ~120 pages. A seeker tries every path — asceticism, wealth, love, the company of the Buddha himself — and finds that no teacher can hand him the answer. Read it early; it will sit underneath all of Domain 13.

books.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
books.author: Robert Pirsig
books.why: An engineer chases the meaning of Quality until it costs him his mind. Written for exactly my kind of thinking — and it is also a warning about exactly my kind of thinking. Difficult, and worth it.

books.title: The Alchemist
books.author: Paulo Coelho
books.why: I will be recommended this constantly, including by Nepali readers. Short and pleasant; not deep. One sitting, then move on.

books.title: Jonathan Livingston Seagull
books.author: Richard Bach
books.why: An hour. Mastery and non-conformity as parable.

clusters.name: Nepali & South Asian Voices
clusters.rationale: 🇳🇵 *My own ground. Do not skip this cluster in favour of Western self-help — this is where reading connects to who I actually am, and I can read these in the original.

books.title: Karnali Blues
books.author: Buddhisagar
books.edition: 2010; English translation by Michael Hutt, Penguin, ~400 pp
books.why: A son and his father in far-western Nepal, from the son's birth to the father's decline. Its publisher and critics call it the most widely read Nepali novel of the last two decades, and the father-son relationship at its centre is the exact relationship my dataset returns to again and again without ever examining it.

books.title: Palpasa Café
books.author: Narayan Wagle
books.why: An artist during the Maoist insurgency. Madan Puraskar winner and a modern Nepali classic — the war as it felt to people who weren't fighting it.

books.title: Seto Dharti
books.author: Amar Neupane
books.why: Tara, married at seven and widowed at nine, across a lifetime at Devghat. Madan Puraskar winner. Read it in the original Nepali; there's also a well-known Shruti Sambeg audio version.

books.title: Arresting God in Kathmandu
books.author: Samrat Upadhyay
books.why: Short stories. Kathmandu in English, unsentimentally, by the first Nepali-born writer widely published in English.

books.title: The Tutor of History
books.author: Manjushree Thapa
books.why: Nepali electoral politics through the lives of ordinary people in a small town.

books.title: A Fine Balance
books.author: Rohinton Mistry
books.why: India during the Emergency. Devastating, and one of the great novels of the subcontinent.

books.title: Midnight's Children
books.author: Salman Rushdie
books.why: Independence and Partition as magic realism. Booker of Bookers.

books.title: Crime and Punishment
books.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
books.why: A brilliant, isolated young man reasons his way into a monstrous act and then cannot live with it. The definitive novel about intellect untethered from conscience — and about a mind that thinks its way into a corner.

books.title: East of Eden
books.author: John Steinbeck
books.why: Inheritance, choice, and* timshel *— "thou mayest." The most hopeful book on this entire list, and the strongest argument that character is chosen rather than inherited.

books.title: The Brothers Karamazov
books.author: Dostoevsky
books.why: Faith, doubt, patricide, freedom. A year-long project, not a book.

books.title: Norwegian Wood
books.author: Haruki Murakami
books.why: Loss, grief and young adulthood. Quiet and melancholy.

books.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
books.author: Gabriel García Márquez
books.why: A family across a century, and the novel that made magic realism.

clusters.name: Light Fiction for Rest
clusters.rationale: For a bad week. **This counts.** No guilt attached, no action items required.

books.title: A Man Called Ove
books.author: Fredrik Backman
books.why: Grief, stubbornness and community. Warm and funny, and quietly about a man who cannot ask for help.

books.title: The Midnight Library
books.author: Matt Haig
books.why: Regret and the lives not lived. Directly relevant to a fear of "not achieving everything," and light enough to read in two sittings.

books.title: Project Hail Mary
books.author: Andy Weir
books.why: Pure engineer joy. Problem-solving as a page-turner. Read when I need to remember that thinking is fun.

books.title: Shoe Dog
books.author: Phil Knight
books.why: The most honest founder memoir written: Nike as eighteen years of near-bankruptcy and self-doubt rather than a triumph montage. The correct antidote to startup mythology and to the highlight reels I'll compare myself against.

books.title: Educated
books.author: Tara Westover
books.why: Self-education as escape, and as cost. What learning does to a person's relationship with their family.

books.title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
books.why: The original self-improvement system: thirteen virtues, tracked daily on a chart, by a man who cheerfully admits he never mastered them. **Note how lightly he holds his own failures.** That, not the chart, is the lesson.

books.title: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
books.author: M.K. Gandhi
books.why: Self-discipline, diet, celibacy, honesty — pursued to an extreme and reported without flattery. A South Asian model of self-improvement that predates the entire Western genre, including its excesses.

books.title: Long Walk to Freedom
books.author: Nelson Mandela
books.why: Twenty-seven years, and what survived them.

books.title: Steve Jobs
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.why: Read for the product judgement. **Not** as a model for how to treat people — the book is quite clear about that, even when its readers aren't.

clusters.name: Nepal — History & the Present Republic
clusters.rationale: Everything my career, money and family plans sit on top of.

books.title: A History of Nepal
books.author: John Whelpton
books.why: The standard one-volume English history: the Shah unification, the Rana autocracy, 1951, the Panchayat years, the 1990 restoration, the insurgency, the royal massacre. Start here — everything else in this domain assumes it.

books.title: Battles of the New Republic
books.author: Prashant Jha
books.why: Part reportage, part history, part memoir: war to peace, monarchy to republic, Hindu kingdom to secular state. Reported from both Kathmandu's power corridors and the Tarai. The best single account of the transition I grew up inside.

books.title: The Nepal Nexus
books.author: Sudheer Sharma
books.why: An inside account of the Maoists, the palace and New Delhi, by a leading Nepali editor. Originally* Prayogshala *— read it in Nepali if I can.

books.title: Forget Kathmandu: An Elegy for Democracy
books.author: Manjushree Thapa
books.why: History, the royal massacre, and a journey through the war-affected west. Personal and political at once.

books.title: The Rise of the House of Gorkha
books.author: Ludwig F. Stiller
books.why: How Prithvi Narayan Shah welded dozens of small kingdoms into one state — and therefore where Nepali nationalism actually comes from.

clusters.name: The Kathmandu Valley & Newar Civilisation
clusters.rationale: My own people, studied properly rather than assumed.

books.title: Nepal Mandala: A Cultural Study of the Kathmandu Valley
books.author: Mary Shepherd Slusser
books.why: The definitive study of Newar civilisation in the Valley: art, architecture, religion, and cultural history, from over a decade of fieldwork. A reference to live with, not to finish. Borrowable via the Internet Archive.

books.title: Kathmandu
books.author: Thomas Bell
books.why: A long-resident journalist's portrait of the city — its history, politics, layers and contradictions. The readable companion to Slusser's scholarship.

clusters.name: The Neighbourhood — India, China & Being Between Them
clusters.rationale: A landlocked country between two of the largest economies on earth. My career, currency, and business options are all shaped by this whether I study it or not.

books.title: India After Gandhi
books.author: Ramachandra Guha
books.why: The definitive history of the modern Indian republic. Long, and it explains the country whose politics and economy most directly shape Nepal's.
books.clusterName: The Neighbourhood — India, China & Being Between Them

books.title: Age of Ambition
books.author: Evan Osnos
books.why: National Book Award winner. Fortune, truth and faith in the new China, told through individual lives rather than statistics.
books.clusterName: The Neighbourhood — India, China & Being Between Them

clusters.name: The Century I'll Actually Live In

books.title: Factfulness
books.author: Hans Rosling
books.why: Ten instincts that distort how we see global development — and why the world is, on most measures, improving faster than the news suggests. A useful corrective for an anxious, news-avoidant reader who still wants an accurate picture.
books.clusterName: The Century I'll Actually Live In

clusters.name: Why I Procrastinate
clusters.rationale: Diagnosis before tactics. Skipping this is why discipline advice has never stuck.

books.title: The Now Habit
books.author: Neil Fiore
books.why: Procrastination as an anxiety response to perfectionist pressure, not a character flaw. My book.

books.title: Solving the Procrastination Puzzle
books.author: Timothy Pychyl
books.why: Short, research-based, zero fluff. Pychyl is the academic who established procrastination as an emotion-regulation problem.

books.title: The War of Art
books.author: Steven Pressfield
books.why: Names the enemy "Resistance." One hour, quotable, useful on a bad morning.

books.title: Do Hard Things
books.author: Steve Magness
books.why: Real toughness vs. self-punishment. The antidote if discipline starts feeling like penance.

books.title: Atomic Habits
books.author: James Clear
books.why: "Identity-based habits" is already in my hierarchy. This is the source. Use it to build the reading habit itself.

books.title: Tiny Habits
books.author: BJ Fogg
books.why: Behaviour design for when motivation is simply unavailable — which is most days.

books.title: The Power of Habit
books.author: Charles Duhigg
books.why: More journalism than method. Skip unless I want the stories.

clusters.name: Attention, Dopamine & Digital Discipline
clusters.rationale: My named momentum-killer — it appears three separate times in my own dataset. This cluster also covers compulsive use of any high-dopamine input, which is the honest home for the "sexual energy" question my hierarchy raises.

books.title: Dopamine Nation
books.author: Anna Lembke
books.why: A Stanford addiction psychiatrist on the pleasure-pain balance. Covers compulsion across every input — phone, porn, food, work — with one mechanism.

books.title: Deep Work
books.author: Cal Newport
books.why: How to actually get and protect the 2–4 hour blocks I say I want.

books.title: Digital Minimalism
books.author: Cal Newport
books.why: The 30-day declutter protocol. Do it, don't just read it.

books.title: Indistractable
books.author: Nir Eyal
books.why: Internal triggers + timeboxing. A practical counterweight to Newport's absolutism.

books.title: Stolen Focus
books.author: Johann Hari
books.why: Systemic argument — attention as something taken, not lost. Good context, thin on action.

books.title: Peak Performance
books.author: Stulberg & Magness
books.why: Stress + rest = growth. Reframes discipline as energy management, which is closer to how I actually work.

books.title: Rest
books.author: Alex Soojung-Kim Pang
books.why: Rest as a deliberate skill, not a reward to be earned. Aimed at people who feel guilty stopping.

books.title: The Willpower Instinct
books.author: Kelly McGonigal
books.why: Built substantially on ego-depletion research that has failed replication. The exercises are still useful; the underlying theory should be held loosely.

books.title: Four Thousand Weeks
books.author: Oliver Burkeman
books.why: The direct, serious answer to my own sentence: "life would feel wasted if I don't achieve everything I want." Read it before I build another decade on that belief.

books.title: Essentialism
books.author: Greg McKeown
books.why: "Less but better." Repetitive, but the message lands.

books.title: Getting Things Done
books.author: David Allen
books.why: A capture system, not a philosophy. Open it when inputs overflow.

books.title: Make Time
books.author: Knapp & Zeratsky
books.why: Light and tactical. Good for a low-energy week.

clusters.name: Designing Life as a System
clusters.rationale: My Level 11 meta-layer, made readable.

books.title: The 12 Week Year
books.author: Brian Moran
books.why: Annual goals fail because twelve months is too long to feel urgency. Twelve-week cycles fix my planning horizon.

domains.name: MIND & EMOTIONAL ARCHITECTURE
domains.question: Can I live inside my own head?

books.title: Mindset
books.author: Carol Dweck
books.why: I use the phrase "growth mindset" seven times across my documents. Read the source — especially the material on **false growth mindset**, which is adopting the vocabulary without the practice. Worth checking myself against honestly.

books.title: Self-Compassion
books.author: Kristin Neff
books.why: Research-based, not soft. Neff's central finding is that self-compassion outperforms self-criticism on actual achievement — which contradicts how I currently motivate myself.

books.title: How to Be an Imperfectionist
books.author: Stephen Guise
books.why: Small, concrete exposure exercises. Cheap to read, easy to start.

books.title: The Gifts of Imperfection
books.author: Brené Brown
books.why: Letting go of who I think I'm supposed to be.

books.title: Chatter
books.author: Ethan Kross
books.why: The science of the inner voice and how to quiet it. Written for analytical internal processors — which is precisely how I described myself.

books.title: The Happiness Trap
books.author: Russ Harris
books.why: ACT in plain language. The origin of "psychological flexibility," a term already sitting in my hierarchy.

books.title: Rewire Your Anxious Brain
books.author: Pittman & Karle
books.why: Amygdala vs. cortex pathways. Mechanism-level, which an engineer's mind finds satisfying rather than patronising.

books.title: Feeling Good
books.author: David Burns
books.why: The CBT workbook. Use it on one stuck thought pattern, not as a read-through.

clusters.name: Emotional Literacy
clusters.rationale: I left "what emotion do you suppress most?" blank in my own dataset. That blank is the finding, not an oversight.

books.title: Atlas of the Heart
books.author: Brené Brown
books.why: 87 emotions, precisely distinguished. A reference for the vocabulary my hierarchy says I want ("naming emotions").

books.title: Permission to Feel
books.author: Marc Brackett
books.why: The RULER method. Systematic and staged, which suits how I learn.

books.title: Emotional Intelligence
books.author: Daniel Goleman
books.why: Foundational and worth knowing, but the popular claim that EQ predicts success far more than IQ is not well supported by the evidence. Take the framework, not the statistics.

clusters.name: Shadow, Origins & Self-Knowledge
clusters.rationale: Optional. Open only if something in 2.3 hits a nerve. Do not manufacture a wound in order to be thorough — that would be perfectionism wearing a therapy costume.

books.title: Owning Your Own Shadow
books.author: Robert A. Johnson
books.why: 90 pages. The clearest short entry to "shadow integration," which my hierarchy names without defining.

books.title: Maybe You Should Talk to Someone
books.author: Lori Gottlieb
books.why: A therapist in therapy. The gentlest possible introduction to the idea, for someone who processes everything alone.

books.title: No Bad Parts
books.author: Richard Schwartz
books.why: Internal Family Systems. Useful if the inner critic feels like a separate voice.

books.title: The Body Keeps the Score
books.author: Bessel van der Kolk
books.why: Heavy, and widely over-recommended. Only if trauma is genuinely live for me.

books.title: Daring Greatly
books.author: Brené Brown
books.why: Vulnerability as strength rather than exposure. Relevant to a home where affection was, in my own word, "practical."

clusters.name: Meditation as a System
clusters.rationale: Technical, staged, falsifiable. No charisma, no personal brand, nothing being sold.

books.title: The Mind Illuminated
books.author: Culadasa (John Yates)
books.why: Ten stages with clear diagnostics and troubleshooting. Engineering-grade precision — the best meditation manual for a mind like mine.

books.title: Mindfulness in Plain English
books.author: Bhante Gunaratana
books.why: Free online, in full. No mysticism, no theatre, no teacher to trust.

books.title: Why Buddhism Is True
books.author: Robert Wright
books.why: Evolutionary psychology meets meditation. No faith required at any point.

books.title: Waking Up
books.author: Sam Harris
books.why: Contemplative practice with zero metaphysical claims attached.

books.title: 10% Happier
books.author: Dan Harris
books.why: A skeptic's memoir. Read only if I need permission before beginning.

clusters.name: Sleep & Circadian Rhythm
clusters.rationale: The 4:30–5:00am wake I want is only sustainable if this side is solved first.

books.title: Why We Sleep
books.author: Matthew Walker
books.why: The best single case for sleep as the foundation of everything else.

books.title: The Circadian Code
books.author: Satchin Panda
books.why: Light timing and eating windows, from a circadian researcher. Reference-grade.

books.title: Bigger Leaner Stronger
books.author: Michael Matthews
books.why: One complete, evidence-based program for a male lifter. Follow it and stop reading about training — the reading is the procrastination.

books.title: Built to Move
books.author: Kelly & Juliet Starrett
books.why: Ten mobility tests and the work to pass them. Directly serves "posture as confidence" and desk damage.

books.title: Starting Strength
books.author: Mark Rippetoe
books.why: Technique reference for the main barbell lifts. Consult chapters; don't read it through.

books.title: Endure
books.author: Alex Hutchinson
books.why: Where physical limits actually come from — mostly the brain. Good if my stamina concern is real.

clusters.name: Nutrition, Fasting & Longevity
clusters.rationale: 💡 *Context note: nearly all nutrition books assume a Western food environment. Dal-bhat, seasonal Nepali produce, and a South Asian metabolic profile all change the specifics. Take the principles — protein sufficiency, fibre, whole foods, meal timing — and rebuild the plan locally.

books.title: Outlive
books.author: Peter Attia
books.why: Healthspan over lifespan. The serious version of my "longevity mindset" — a framework and a set of markers, not a diet.

books.title: The Hungry Brain
books.author: Stephan Guyenet
books.why: Why eating goes wrong at the brain level. Removes moral judgement from food, which matters given how I talk to myself.

books.title: The Complete Guide to Fasting
books.author: Jason Fung
books.why: "Fasting protocols" from my hierarchy, with the physiology. Fung is a nephrologist with strong views; read the mechanism, hold the certainty loosely.

books.title: Breath
books.author: James Nestor
